description:
Sponsor: Montech King 95 Pro on Amazon https://geni.us/C5P2
The NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti is the Greatest GPU of All Time thanks to a mix of value, performance, and timing on a market teeming with excellent choices. It was an era when the AMD RX 580 was largely competing in the mid-range with the GTX 1060, Vega hadn't yet launched, and Intel Arc didn't even exist as a thought in anyone's mind. In this 2024 revisit & benchmark of the GTX 1080 Ti & GTX 1080 (non-Ti), we're looking at performance today and how it compares to modern graphics cards. Upgrades on the NVIDIA side might include the RTX 4070 Ti Super or RTX 4070 Super if spending less, or maybe an RTX 4080 Super for more; on the AMD side, that is more likely an RX 7900 XT or RX 7900 XTX, or possibly the "new" GRE (with its global launch). The GTX 1080 Ti and 1080 Pascal architecture GPUs can't reasonably handle real-time ray tracing, so obviously those charts are absent. A modern card is effectively infinitely better. But for rasterization, they still hang in there.

This video gives some of the history and some personal thoughts, opinions, and memories on the Pascal era.

There are some, ehem, off brand drivers that enable rtx on 1080 series cards, you should try it. As a side note, I will run at least one 1080 to drive extra monitors until the latest OS doesn't understand what it is. The 1080 is one of THE most efficient cards ever, with enough oompf to still play vr games. It's a shame nvidia disabled sli, and turning it on for compatible games is such a hassle, because I run two 1080s, on water, with a passive radiator..... My computer has 1 fan. Because there is not a 100% liquid cooled power supply I can afford. However, the power supply is so woefully under utilized, that I can't hear that fan, over the gentle humm of my water pump. It's like I have fish tank next to me instead of a pc, without the gentle water noises. That is the greatness of the 1080, gaming with 60-80 watts. It takes more power to light a large room, than run superposition.... Less power, less heat, less noise, less money to operate.

1080ti, honorable mention. Yes faster, but almost twice the power, and at that point, why not 5700xt or 6700xt. I like my AMDs.

Currently writing this on my GTX 1070 Laptop at uni, which from experience still runs fine in a lot of popular games. My first PC I built had a Titan Xp (With DVI), and that thing was a BEAST! From my knowledge it was like 2-5% better performance over the 1080 Ti which made many Titan Xp owners angry when their card cost 2x as much as the 1080 Ti. But i got the Titan for around $160-170 during the height of the GPU crisis, so I considered it a win. I remember being able to force RT on in a few games, and while it wasn't great, it was noticeably working in reflections and didn't impact my gaming because the TV I played on has a refresh rate of 30 hz, or my parents connected an old HDMI cable to it. It still got 30+ FPS in every game at native 4K with highest settings, and Star Wars: Jedi Survivor was one that I could force RT on with everything else and it ran fine. 

Don't get one of these expecting RT performance, I'm just saying these things are so powerful that sometimes it CAN (Not always) brute-force RT in some titles

comments.text:
Good stuff as always. Good luck with the PayPal suit.

My upgrade path went - GTX 480 > 660Ti > 780Ti > 1080Ti. The 1080Ti has been a solid performer for me for 7 years running both a Pimax 4K (the reason for the upgrade 780Ti to 1080Ti) well and a Pimax 5K Plus adequately, and for the majority of that time running a 4K display and a 1080p display as dual screens, giving me an average spend per year of around £60  for a GPU (I bought a used  EBay bargain EVGA GTX 1080Ti in early 2018). I peg my GPU and CPU budget at around £400 - £450 for each so I look at each generation and decide is there a GPU or CPU will that would give me 75 - 80% performance at 50% the cost and maintain that for 4 - 5 years in that price range. 

Your shows and others like it are very useful in making my assessment of when, how and what to consider as my next upgrade, I'm sure you've helped a lot of people get the best bang for the buck over the years. I'm all about average cost per year, I've had a Logitech C920 for 13 years now using it almost every day and it's very unlikely I'll be replacing it any time soon.

This time I went new with SCAN's £430 (it's 20% VAT here) XFX RX 7800XT mainly because NVidia has announced it is ending driver support for the GTX 1000 series and it's beginning to struggle (or I'm losing patience) with the later versions of Blender and DAZ3D. I'm still waiting for the RX 7800XT to be delivered. I'm hoping to stick with AM4 and 'upgrade' my 3900X to a used 5800X3D for Windows compatibility when I can snag one, I'll probably stick with AM4 for a good while yet after all the crazy Intel switching sockets it was a no brainer to switch to Ryzen for me. By selling the 780Ti and the 1080Ti as well as the 3900X I hope to recoup a substantial amount of the upgrade cost.

I mostly use my GPU for 3D creation stuff, I still have the Pimax 5K Plus which I got half price in mint condition because they thought it had stopped working, they had messed up a firmware upgrade, it took 10 minutes to fix, some video encoding and playing older games, though like you I'm also into Star Citizen... so there's that... How would you feel about a Squadron 42 benchmark? I'll be more than happy if the RX 7800XT gives the same performance and longevity as the venerable GTX 1080Ti.

comments.text: I have 2 1080TI FE cards in SLI, I retired them for a 3090.  That was not an upgrade for me.  The 3090 is now on its 3rd (yes I'm saying 3x) RMA for completely dieing.  And the 3090 is still under warranty.  It dies, I send it back, they send me a different one.  This one lasted about 2 weeks.  Every time the 3090 dies, I put the 1080TI SLI cards back in and they just work. I OC the shit out the 1080TIs, they don't care, they always work reliably and perform for me playing FO4 and Skyrim both in 4k with a ton of mods.  The 3090 barely (as in not by much at all, not significantly) has more FPS. Usually they are within 2 or 3 in the same areas of the maps.  Yes, the 1080TI SLI is the GOAT, yes it requires a massive PSU, yes it will make your computer room hot (650 watts of heat comes out of them continuously), yes they take up a lot of space in the case, but they are worth it for me and the types of games I play. I had 2x Gigabyte 1080s back in 2016. Bought them for $550 each off Newegg and had them paired up with the equally legendary Intel 2600K CPU that I got on release for $200 back in 2013. Had them both running gloriously in SLI when that was still a thing. Was on that system until I upgraded to an MSI 2080ti. I got the 2080ti somehow though a deal on ebay for $700 so it was too good to pass up at the start of 2019. I paired that GPU up eventually with a 3950x AMD processor as well in 2019 when it was release which was finally an upgrade to my 2600K after 6 years. The only reason I don't have those video cards anymore was because when Covid was coming, bitcoin mining was the craze, and GPU's were scarce those factors made the the used price on all those cards sky rocket. So I sold them for double of the price I paid because I could. Sold the 1080s for $1000 each and the 2080ti for $1600. Funny thing is someone sold me on release day their PNY 3090 for $1500 at the same time. Yah it was cheaper that release MSRP and without tax. Brand new in the box. I am still flabbergasted by how that turned out. Truth be told, when the guy was selling it I thought it was somehow already broken, fake, or I would be shot for my money. I've been using the 3090 since. I didn't see a compelling reason to upgrade to the 4xxx series. Was hoping the current AMD 9xxx series CPU and the latest GPUs would be more compelling this release than what they are over my 5950x and 3090. For the prices I am still sticking with what I got.

Still, I had many great hours on those 1080s.

comments.text: GPU speeds are increasing at the rate of about 9% a year, while CPU speeds are increasing at the rate of about 28% a year. Over the years, I have observed that the minimum increase to be noticeable in everyday use ("oh, this is more responsive") is about 30%. Improvements smaller than that can be measured with a timer, but you don't really notice them, so there is no reason to upgrade for less than a 30% improvement. These days, I upgrade when I can get a 2-300% percent improvement (long ago was 1000%). With the current rates of improvement, upgrade your CPU every 3-4 years, and your GPU every 8-12 years. A 1080 Ti should be upgraded by 2029.

comments.text:
You know, I used to like to doing "flagship" build every 5 to 10 years, sometimes sooner than 5 years if I'm feeling wasteful. I decided (stupidly) to do it in late 2020.

I went from a 7700K, 32GB RAM 1080Ti to an Ryzen 9 5950X, 64GB of RAM, and an RTX 3090.

Not worth it at all and I wish I kept my money. The 1080 Ti kicked ass for the games I was playing and the resolution I was using.

Getting the 3090 is what got me to upgrade from 1080p 144Hz to 1440p 144Hz, go multi-monitor, and drive a 4K TV which the 1080 Ti would've struggled with. But it was the upgrade that drove me to more uneccessary upgrades and now really feels like a post-hoc justification of the PC upgrade.

If what you have works, stick with it. In 2025 it'll have been the 5 year mark and I am so happy to hold on to what I have now.

My philosophy going forward is no longer to build a flagship machine every 5 or even 10 years. Instead it will be to wait until the midrange can far and away beat what I currently have AND it's available in decent condition used.

EDIT: I still have that 1080 Ti system in pieces and boxed up in the original parts and I'll never get rid of it because it marks a really nice era in PC building and means even more to me than the previous flagship PC (3770k, Radeon HD 7970 GHz edition, 16GB DDR3). Usually I sell the old parts to upgrade but this time I didn't need to and I'm so glad to hold on to it.

comments.text:
You're very obviously a nvidia fanboy and I've gathered that from watching various videos from you. But the thing about amd is that it was almost always the budget option between the two. And when there was more competition than the 2 (and before intel) it was always second best option. You'd prefer an amd card if you couldn't get a nvidia card, over anything else. 

But most importantly is that amd's cards have always had a solid market outside of windows gaming. Like productivity on linux has always, always, always, always preferred amd over nvidia even where nvidia is preferred (Davinci Resolve for example which is built to only be utilized with nvidia) but the open source community, with open source drivers and amd's open source nature in general, has always had its foothold. And you're looking at this almost exclusively in the like guise of the first world. For someone in like Brazil in the 00s or early 2010s, who would never in their life afford a new nvidia card, amd was amazing and phenomonal. Not everyone cares about ultra raytracing 4k gaming. Most people game in 1080p. Some people still game in 720p. It's always a type of person like you that looks at this like "the 1080 ti was the best thing ever omg," but I grew up very extremely poor and a linux user that built my comptuers from pcs people threw in their garbage. AMD will always have a special place in my heart and there will never be a time when they cannot come back as the underdog. In fact AMD's 5800x3d and 7800x3D has FAR redeemed any down failures they've had in the gaming market. The ryzen series is so good that intel wouldn't put out anything comparable or even remotely worth it. Upgrading the a ryzen 7k series cpu had the biggest impact on gaming over anything else (I doubled ram, I doubled benchmark of cards and everythig you can think of,) and the 8000x3d will likely have a competitor from intel (finally) but in combination with their affordable cards that do great (you don't need 200 fps in 4k, I know this is heart breaking to nvidia stans but you're just looking for reasons to validate your purchase aka waste of money.) 

But also nvidia drivers literally shorted my last pc. I was always a amd fangirl but after nvidia fucked me like that and I had to build a new pc, I've swore to NEVER buy a card unless it's for work. And frankly for productivity I'd probably just get a mid range nvidia card and ONLY if I have to for my job. If a amd card will do it and I can stay on linux then I will not touch a nvidia card ever again

The 1080ti is the goat of the past eight years at best. 

Those absolutely terrible eight years that have seen GPUs becoming more and more expensive -- whilst screens, storage, memory and even CPUs such a current gen Ryzen have just the same price tag as 15-20 years ago. In other words, the years where GPU manufacturing progress got pretty much axed: "The more you buy, the more you save!" By the way: Tech channels adjusting historical GPU prices for inflation 1:1 are doing company PR work for free.

Firstly: One reason why Pascal lasted so long is because it was released when new consoles were a good few years away. Ever since PS5/XBox Series X hit the market in 2020, more and more are hitting the minimum requirements, or falling below that, starting with GTX 1060/1070. Speaking of which, nobody would still be on Pascal if prices hadn't become that terrible. Alan Wake 2 wrecks the 1080ti as well.

Secondly:  The actually GOAT are both the GeForce 4ti 4200. As well as the GeForce 8800 GT.

Both offering performance near the top end respectively -- at but a fraction of the cost. And THAT's a mistake that Nvidia is not gonna make for SURE. :-)

comments.text:
I disagree that the 7900XTX can be a 1080Ti equivalent nowadays. At a $700-800 price, I agree, but for $1,000, the price bracket is simply too high IMO for a reasonable PC build, and is squarely in wealthy enthusiast territory. The 1080Ti was still meant to have a reasonable value, even if the 1070 or 1080 were better for dollar-per-FPS or a similar metric. For $1,000 though, I think that puts the 7900XTX (without any sales) out of the exact same class as the 1080Ti
The cost of PC building shouldn't directly scale with inflation. DIY PCs are, in a sense, hobby machines. The price of those should tend to stay constant for the same relative price tier. $300 for an ultra-budget PC, $700-800 for a mid-range PC, and $1,500-2,000 for a high-end PC, or something similar to that. It shouldn't increase so rapidly alongside the many other price jumps on more critical items, unless people will also fall out of this hobby and leave this industry to wither away.

comments.text:
If Nvidia released a dual-slot AD102-based card with a TDP of 225 or 375W and equipped with DisplayPort 2.0, it would be the next GOAT. The 4090 is great, but its default power consumption and oversized cooler (even for its nominal TDP) make it impractical for a lot of builds. The 4090's AD102 is essentially a consumer version of the H100 that powers ChatGPT and other AI models. Nvidia makes something like 1000% profit margins on those, so it's not surprising they're dedicating less complex and lower-binned chips to gaming GPUs. I'm not sure why they went with DP 1.4a (repurposing the 30-series tech or planned obsolescence), but that's the only thing that makes the 4090 less than future-proof.
A dual-slot 4090 with DP2.0 would be a useful gaming GPU for a decade or more.

comments.text:
The RT generations have been plagued by a catch-22 at the low end. Enable upscaling and sacrifice performance but get some visual quality... and then immediately lose quality because 1080p is rough on fidelity when upscaled. But then go to a higher res without RT and not have enough VRAM. It's why the 1080 Ti can still exist, just turn off RT and you'll still have enough RAM for any playable resolution. AMD missed the boat by not undercutting Nvidia and going for the jugular by emphasizing RAM and rasterization. But they played soft and have been losing because their prices haven't been competitive enough.

In many ways, their 6000 series with 16 GB can compete more than well enough at rasterization while coming in as a low cost refresh product. With the 7000 series so mediocre--they may as well have. 

There's so much to say on upscaling, VRAM, Rt, and performance. I feel that we, as buyers are getting the short end of the stick by getting overpriced cards that don't perform worthwhile for the "features" that are touted, or if they do it's only halo products with upscaling yadayada.

comments.text:
@GamersNexus

I'm still plenty happy with my EVGA GTX1080Ti FTW3, there are multiple reasons why this thing is still kicking today.
And since release it has been running on a 117% Powertarget drawing up to 320W with 1949Mhz stable clockspeed throughout any game.

REASON 1: the availability and price points.
With the newer GPU's launching, they often did not come with a better price point and due to the crypto-problems availability became an issue.

REASON 2: the VRAM budget
One of the biggest reasons that this card is still surviving to this date is because of it's massive VRAM budget at the time.
Granted, not every game will fully utilize it, but being closer to the edge of the limit usually comes with framepacing instability due to swapping.

Quite some of the newer cards still only come with 8GB, or 12GB etc. and that just didn't feel like a justification for an upgrade.
We don't only play games that snoop away from the VRAM budget, but what to think of browsers in the background, or editing a bunch of photo's at once in applications like paint net quickly will add up on the VRAM budget.

Anyone remember the Fury X debacle with it only having 4GB VRAM? We almost forgotten it even ever existed...
Which brings me to another point, maybe retest the Fury X 4GB and the 980Ti 6GB and see how it upholds to this date.

Ontop of tha regarding VRAM, now having swapped from DWM-less Windows 7 to Windows 10, the VRAM budget is increasingly used especially when browsers have a few tabs open in the background, we no longer idle at maybe 150-200MB VRAM like we used to, it gets quickly closer to 1GB or more.

Hogwarts Legacy and Ratchet & Clank Rifts Apart still play beautifully with this card, especially with G-sync combined with it at 1440P.
These games take quite a lot of VRAM almost to 11GB which perfectly suits this card still.

REASON 3: the raw rasterization performance
While some of the most modern titles will start to become an issue, plenty of games still do not utilize RTX and it is also not mandatory.
Like the aforementioned Hogwarts Legacy and Ratchet & Clank Rifts Apart being probably one of the most recent playable titles on Ultra settings at 1440P combined with G-sync.

Halo Infinite would have to run on low settings but still churns out beyond 100fps combined with a i9 13900K, my old i7 3930K at 4.4Ghz would struggle to get beyond 30fps in that game due to CPU utilization pegged at 100%, Battlefield V was the last game that CPU could properly pull off with 100+FPS at 85-95% CPU utilization in Ultra.

Even GTA V has seen an uplift from the i7 3930k to the i9 13900k combined with the GTX1080Ti FTW3 due to the fact the distance sliders basically having no impact on performance due to the extra CPU head-room, and due to this the old GPU was able to churn out more frames at a better fidelity it could ever before.

If you do not need ray-tracing perse, it is still a great contender, and it still performs well in titles like World of Warcraft too!

REASON 4: build quality/durability
Well this is an obvious one, you already made a video about the exceptional build quality/engineering of this FTW3 videocard, and it goes to show that after 7 years of daily intensive use, the card is still not showing a single sign of failure, degradation or noise problems. It still works like day 1!

And what is even funnier, my videocard is still 3 more years in warranty...

REASON 5: Displayport
The RTX4090 is quite another league of it's own compared to the 1080Ti, but it does not justify the cost in my opinion, while I did find 24GB VRAM a little on the low side for a full-blown upgrade at that price point, another problem being Displayport 1.4a is still being employed on these videocards.

Which is a shame, because performance wise they can easily drive 4K 120Hz+ displays but their connector is not up to it without adding compression. So the RTX 5090 will be our next viable station with DisplayPort 2.1 and GDDR7 with increased memory-bandwidths which will also aid in higher resolution workloads.


OTHER THINGS I'D LIKE TO MENTION:
1: Your graphs show ReBar being enabled, but the 1000-series doesn't support it, without it the results might've been closer.

2: The FTW3 card on overclock by default only goes to 320W tops, even if you enable the OC bios that would supposedly give it up to 127% powertarget headroom which would theoretically allow it to draw up to 355.6W.
However, due to Nvidia's limitations, the videocard is still bottlenecked because it only allows up to 320W power-draw, despite the 127% setting.

Vince (Kingpin) Lucido had on their kingpincooling forums released 'secret' VBIOS versions for a few 1080Ti cards that would work around this power-budget problem, so you would have to flash this bios in order to get a higher power-budget headroom to play with.

The forums however are down for a long time, BUT, back then  managed to preserve this page & bios downloads using the waybackmachine!

In order to find these files you will have to google the following EVGA forums topic:
"1080 TI FTW3 watercooled Slave BIOS doesn't go over 117%"

Then put the links into the waybackmachine and you should be good to go! (see page 3 under Sajin's post)
But you can ofcourse also use the mediafire hosted links on the forum topic itself.

Such a shame EVGA stepped out of the market, this giant will be missed forever.

I think the most important comparison to really show how good the 1080Ti was is not what card you can buy with the same money in 2024, but rather: 

The proportional performance the 1080Ti brought compared to the other GPUs of that generation and how well it ran the most demanding games of that generation, VS, the proportional performance the same amount of money could buy you in 2024 compared to other GPUs of this generation and how well those cards run the most demanding games of this generation. 

What we will see is the 1080Ti not only dominated its entire generation of GPUs, it also pretty much dominated the most demanding games in its generation, up to 1440p, at NATIVE resolutions without upscaling. For comparison, the 4070Ti Super and 4080 Super are not nearly as dominant within the current GPU stack and absolutely cannot run the most demanding games at the highest settings, at 1440p native. 

The only card that provides the same proportional dominance in this generation is the 4090 and it costs more than twice of what the 1080Ti would have cost. And it STILL requires upscaling to achieve that dominance in the most demanding games of this generation.

comments.text:
Im gonna call it and get hated for it.

The 1080ti did nothing performance wise , than the 4090 didn’t 

Both made a MASSIVE ABSURD JUMP from the last gen.
Both were MILES AHEAD of any other GPU at their respective times.

And both were cheaper than the last gen top card (3090ti 2,000$ - 4090 1599$)

The difference why the 1080ti got legendary status and the 4090 probably most likely won’t , were pure external factors.

1) as mentioned in the video , terrible , like absolutely shit show of a 2000 series launch. RTX gpus with no features or games to feature them and milf dissapointing raw performance increase.

2)Launched in the middle of a console generation, it’s no secret by now that consoles are the most important market for game developers and hence why games are optimized for them , so consoles kind of dictate how demanding games are because usually , pc versions are the console game with the option to crank some settings higher , but very similar base line.

When gpus launch in the middle of a console generation, they get games optimized for 3-4 year old consoles that are equiparable to middle end 4 year old hardware. And still have 3-4 years to go before the next one launches.

3) On top of being launched in the middle of a console generation, the pandemic , plus scalpers and several situations in 2020, caused a very slow and progressive introduction of the new console generation with lots of stock issues. Because of this we saw a long intergenerational gap of nearly 2 years , where games kept being “made” and “designed” for the old consoles with the new lens just getting higher resolution and frame rate. It wasn’t till middle 2022 that we started to see some real Next gen only titles.
Wich extended the 1080ti’s glory anooother 1 and half years.

4) if all this wasn’t enough there’s a situation when only high end gpus are really making big jumps but low end gpus are making very small intergenerational jumps. And since this GpUs kind of have to run games too, the 1080ti keeps relevant for even longer.

And last but not least. In fact I’d say this is the most important and most deciding factor.
Resolution.

1080p PC gaming became a thing at about 2006 it existed before but that’s when it started becoming quite popular.

And it was an era of one res fits all.

The GTX 1000 series didn’t launched aimed at 3 different resolutions depending on tier.

They all did 1080p res , just some better than others.
3xxxx series didn’t had this luck.
They weren’t even given the courtesy of being asked for 1 jump in resolution to 1440p wich is already double the resolution and twice as hard to run.

3080s and 3090s where asked to do 4k
And 3070s and 3060tis to do 1440p
And 3060s and 3050 to slaughter 1080p and of course this was ti much of an ask, making the 1080ti, wich was never asked to do anything above 1080p , look good again.

Can you imagine if 4k wasn’t a thing and the 3090ti was launched exclusively as a 1440p GPU? It would have probably even been considered overkill.
Same thing this gen.

While the 1080ti was asked to run games launched for 4-5 year old consoles with old engines and no new or demanding technology on a 13-14 year old resolution that everyone used.

The 4090 is being asked to do 4k wich is still incredibly demanding, while doing stuff like path tracing wich doesn’t even exists in consoles , or ultra raytracing wich also doesn’t exists on consoles. And using its feature set it manages , and people still says “yah but it isn’t native not impressive “ 😂😂😂😂🤦🏻‍♂️

1080ti had all the external factors aligned to make it legendary, but hardware wise , it isn’t one bit more impressive than some other gpus that game before or after

comments.text:
For me, the 3090ti was the greatest.  Even JTC said that it will take two or three generations for a single card to outperform the 3090ti in SLI and I agree with him.  Past SLI setups never had that much of a performance boost, and the 1080ti in SLI never came close.  Upon its release, the 3090ti was the only card that could get 60+ FPS on the most demanding games with MSAAx8, RT-High @4K simultaneously. In SLI, FPS would be in the 90s.  
11GB of VRAM on the 1080ti was enough back then for graphics-heavy games in 2017, but for today's games at maximum settings, 11GB just isn't going to cut it all of the time.  The 3090ti's 24GBs of VRAM was ahead of it's time, even if the card's clock speeds still weren't fast enough to push that much memory efficiently.  As for price to performance – a Dodge Charger R/T is $50K.  A McLaren is $210K.  The Dodge Charger R/T is a much better car than the McLaren, because you know....price-to-performance.

comments.text:
Sandy Bridge (i5-2600K, i7-2700K). And I'm saying this as someone who is (more) an AMD fan. Nothing else really had quite that reputation of longevity and value as well as overclocking capability; CPUs and GPUs don't leave much on the table anymore, thanks to automatic boosting.

Didn't own one myself, but GN has covered its legendary status before ("10 Years of Intel CPUs Benchmarked" from 3 years ago probably covers it). Only in the past few years has it started to really bottleneck GPUs enough to be retired by most gamers (though I'm sure plenty still using them).

Ryzen - while great for kicking off new CPU core race and value - wasn't quite polished with first gen (AM4 as a platform, though, deserves plenty of recognition). Too many teething issues with Ryzen 1000 and early mobo, RAM issues. Later gens got better in that regard, but It would be hard to name a single part that deserves the honor of "GOAT". The brand/series overall is fantastic, though, and continues to be so on AM5.

A well deserved accolade.  I made a jump to this card from a 970, just as soon as it was released. I think I actually paid slightly less than MSRP (somehow) however, UK pricing and inflation are different.
Why is it the G.O.A.T. for me? It held on for so long compared to the later cards. The 20XX series were way overpriced, RTX was the new snake oil at that time, and even then the 1080Ti was beating the pants off the lower end models (70's and 60's) using only a pillow.  I'm sure it saved gamers a ton of cash over the Great GPU shortage of '21/'22, as there was nothing really worth buying then.
Sadly (with the advent of new games) the upgrade was inevitable. When prices dropped in summer 2022, I ended up getting a 3080 12G. Price to performance for it was good (as well as stability, the 3080Ti's were notorious for needing a firmware updates) and it was the lowest it had ever been for cost. It will never beat the 1080Ti on price to performance though. 

Again, a well deserved accolade.  As for my top 3 nVidia cards I have owned (I have had AMD/Radeon though) 1) 1080Ti  2) 3080 12G 3) Geforce4 4200Ti - XFX edition.

Then I had an issue with that card so I sold it in a PC (not a functional issue — I just didn’t like it), and bought myself a 6650 XT, which, again, is basically a 1080 Ti. When I had an opportunity to upgrade again in April, 2023, there was not a single GPU worth buying to replace the 6650 XT except the RTX 4090. I like my big upgrades, cross-generation, and I did not like the look of the 7900 series at the time. If you stuck it out until now, you are blessed with relatively good options in the 7800 XT, 7900 GRE, competitive AMD pricing in general, and eh — okay options in the 4070 Ti Super and 4080 Super. I am assuming you’re not going to upgrade from a card with 11 GB VRAM to one with 12. If you do, you’re missing how well that 11 GB served you in the past when it was lots, and how well 12 will NOT age. Inflation-adjusted, you should not be looking at sub-$800 cards to replace a 1080 Ti anyway, but I’m guessing a fair few 1080 Ti owners have since bought 3090s or 4090s, and that was a good choice.

My 970 completed 9 years of active gaming service this year and is now running my main dev PC (non-gaming), plugged to a 32" 1440p 120Hz monitor, which runs almost 24x7. The 970 bore the brunt of initial years of my Linux gaming back in 2018, when Vulkan and DXVK were just starting up and not as versatile as in SteamOS today. I played 150+ hours of Dying Light completely on Linux at 1440p with this card, big deal considering how unoptimized Proton was then. Even if I bought it for 1080p gaming (my monitor was so), I used DSR and could run every AAA game at 1440p - Far Cry 4, GTA V, Fallout 4, Divinity Original Sin, Dirt Rally, Doom 4. The last major release it ran without a sweat is Red Dead Redemption (2024).

This "7" class card with 256bit bus (today we get only 192bit bus in that class, the same reason why 3060 is not up to 1080 Ti in many games) was whom 1080 Ti dethroned in the GPU hall of fame.

comments.text:
The GTX 1080 Ti totally deserves to be in a hall of fame together with the Geforce 4 Ti 4200, the Radeon 9500 Pro, the Geforce 8800 GT, and the Radeon HD 7970
All cards that had great performance for the money and aged insanely well.
The Ti 4200 not only outperformed the 5200 but also the 6200
the 9500 Pro could be unlocked to a 9700 Pro and that was at the time the unbeatable fastest card
The 8800 GT released at $200 and came incredibly close to the $400+ 8800 GTX and about 3 times the performance of the $150 8600 GTS. That would be like a RTX 4080 SE (With 4070 Ti Super performance) for the price of a 4060 Ti today.
The HD 7970 had incredible performance and aged so well, FineWine became a fitting description.

Personally I'm still on a 1060 like many millions other users. It still does all I need it to do.

The RX 480/580 that only competes against the 1060 in the midrange market is a bit like how the HD 4870 competed in the midrange market against the GTX 260. An almost perfect repeat actually. Slightly better performance and price at slightly higher power draw and some fewer features. And in both periods both cards from both manufacturers were absolutely viable options.
And the RTX 20 cards were basically a proof of concept that hardware RTX can be a thing, but weren't that amazing at it. It took the following generation for a meaningful performance upgrade.

And crazy to see that the 7900 XTX is almost 4 times as fast in Starfield.

The 1080 TI might be 7 years old. But it's also only 3 generations old. Back then we had new cards yearly, if not more frequently. It's like comparing a 680 against 10 series cards. Or a GTX 285 against GTX 600 cards. So in that regard it does fine.

On the other hand, the inflation adjusted comparison really shows how much prices have increased. A x80 Ti then is a x70 Ti now. Pretty much proof that price-wise all the cards are one tier too high.

comments.text:
My other favourite moment in GPU history was when the ATI (now AMD) 9700 pro came out and caught Nvidia with their pants down HARD. It completely destroyed their upcoming FX5800 Ultra, and shook everything up.

Nvidia tried everything they could think of at the time to dig themselves back out of the hole, ultimately digging themselves a bigger one. 

They overclocked the heck out of the FX5800 Ultra to try and make it keep up with the 9700pro. This ended up requiring an extremely loud obnoxious cooler nicknamed "The Dustbuster." It didn't help, and it was still slower, while running very hot and loud.

They then resorted to releasing driver hacks for benchmarks to actually try and cheat in the benchmark software of the time to pull ahead. It still didn't pull ahead, and they got caught doing it.

Nvidia now basically pretends that card never existed. It was an amusing moment in time where they were caught in their complacency, and punished hard for it. Hopefully something that will happen again some day to bring back more competition in the GPU market for consumers/pricing.

To Nvidia's credit they did actually end up making a funny video of it (you can still find on YouTube), where they made fun of themselves for it. Comparing the cooler to a dentist drill, and being hot enough to grill steaks on.

comments.text: I think the big reason most people don't see it that way is largely due to the fact that most people's wages haven't kept up with inflation.  So when we just say "well, with regards to inflation..." it's completely moot.  People still want a card as good for today's games as the 1080Ti was for it's time at the same price point because ultimately people have at best kept pace in real wage terms in the past several years, but many have actually lost in real wage terms.  Most jobs maybe gave 3% raises per year, whilst most costs inflated over 25% (and yes they stayed that way).  Sure the RATE of inflation dropped, but the actual inflation that was caused by the previous few years' extreme inflation rates didn't disappear, it just became the "new normal" pricing.  So yeah, I'm not surprised, given all that, that the average buyer doesn't see the 7900XTX in anywhere near the same light.  It would have to be around $700 (at most) for people to feel that way about it, especially given it's poor ray tracing performance compared to most 40 series cards.

comments.text:
Pascal efficiency especially in the midrange was good. It's actually the only thing that kept me from upgrading to 20 and 30 series. Thankfully 40 series, for what it's worth, brought the power consumption back down and I finally pulled the trigger.

It's not just TDP or consumption under full load, but rather how the cards behave in less demanding scenarios. Pardon my very limited testing but, you can't make a 2060 sip any less than 60 watts. 1060 and 4070 can easily do that with just an FPS limit.
Furthermore, imposing an aggressive 50% power limit bares no stability penalties like 30 series cards which had power hungry memory chips that starved the core when the limit was set this low. Tested on a 3080 10GB.

So if you value passive cooling or enjoy performance per watt like me, midrange 40 series is actually viable. "It's safe to upgrade my Pascal friends". 4070 can easily output more frames than watts consumed under the right circumstances, be it a power + fps limits (these go hand in hand for latency reasons) and/or in-game settings tweaks. In fact I upgraded my entire system recently to target, on average, a Frames / Total System Wattage ratio greater than 1 with power consumption very similar to consoles actually.

Funny Story with My 1080ti

I haven't been gaming regularly lately, but about two months ago I decided to play Death Stranding. As usual, I first tried it in 4k with everything maxed out, but ended up having to lower the resolution to 2k, and of course, in 2k, I could play with everything maxed out. But then the PC started shutting down, and this only happened with games, so I thought, "Well, your time has come, you're dying." To reinforce this theory, I wasn't aware of the Chrome bug, the one that displays a checkerboard pattern affecting many Win11 users – for me, it was just another sign that the GPU was dying.

I have a friend who had a 3080 Suprim X, he upgraded to an AMD XTX7900, and sold me the 3080. You could say the 3080 it was an upgrade, I just can't swallow the 10GB now. Now I can play my favorite titles in 4k like Senua Hellblade, Modern Warfare, Metro Exodus, and more.

It used to be said that drivers would cap old GPUs, but that didn't happen with the 1080ti – mine was getting better and better, and probably not far behind a 4060.

Now, the funny part, turns out the 1080ti is still working, and I have no idea what happened. It's in my daughter's room, on a B87TUF with an i7 4790 and 16GB of DDR3 on a 1080p monitor, it's simply overkill!!! It plays everything maxed out, but my daughter only plays Roblox :-).

comments.text:
Still running my asus rog strix 1080ti oc edition. Never failed me unlike my asus gtx 670 dcu ii 2gb which started causing problems  3-4 years after purchase but ended up surviving untill 2022, i think the problems with the 670 were mostly related to my system not going well with it, the moment i replaced it with the 1080ti, i never had issues with my system again, which is weird because the 670 worked perfectly fine on my brothers old desktop, he had a 560 which died shortly after i upgraded, so i gave him the 670. 

Literally bought the 1080ti shortly after release, here in my area it was pretty much impossible to find high end cards in local stores, but i managed to find one in my local store, i kept refreshing the search page a few times per day on the website for that store, then this one 1080ti popped up and there was only 1 unit in stock, i went directly to the physical shop, spoke with the owner and said i wanted it. He was amazed there was even inventory for this thing as he had no idea he received a 1080ti. I got the 1 unit from his store, he restocked shortly after with a few more units but i think nobody bought them. I got it cheaper because the website was displaying a lower MSRP for this edition, other stores online were selling the same card for 100-200€ higher. The shop owner said he would keep the price i saw because i really wanted that thing. The other units he had for sale, he put them up for almost 1200€ each, i got mine for ~930€. Other stores were mostly selling for 1100€ price range.

I have no clue how shops/inventry work, but this store is mostly asus, so i assume they have a partnership. Prices are on the high side most of the time. And when i say high, i really mean high, the only reason i was using the store back then is because it is local and i knew the people there.

Not gonna lie, when i bought the 1080ti, i had regrets buying it when the RTX 2000 series came. I had a similar issue with my gtx 670 which i bought a week prior to the 700 series being exposed to the world and then i found out the 760 offered almost the same performance for 120 bucks less vs my gtx 670 back then. But as time went on, i am more glad that i bought the 1080ti back then, the test of time is amazing and i'm loving it, i plan to make the most out of it. I have yet to decide if the future for me is handheld or a minipc approach.

Also i feel like the i7 3770k was similarly awesome on the cpu side. I used one from 2012 to 2022. Only reason i stopped using it because motherboard/ram started having conflicts, which i suspect started happening when my PSU was changed from mid tier to low tier, i used a low tier unstable PSU for a 500+W system, PSU worked for like 11 months untill it started causing issues. My old PSU died in 2021, which was better and could handle the system i have. Then i made the move to go for a gold tier PSU that is ranked up high in terms of quality and performance. RM750 from corsair. I had no knowledge about PSU and thought that using any with a 800W label on the side would work just fine, i learnt it the hardway. I'm lucky the bronze PSU did not fry all my hardware, at one point it was causing sparks on my DP cable going from the 1080ti to the monitor, sparks almost sounded like i was making popcorn, and when i saw that crap happen in real time, i was scared for life on what to do as i did not want to loose my entire system to this anomaly.

PSU was indeed the issue, as i started researching the brand, unit model and performance ranking in tier lists across multiple websites, and it was always labeled as something to avoid or use in low end builds. My build was more of high end and was constantly stressing the PSU, which led to this sparkle event. And yes, the 1080ti survived all of this. All of the hardware survived this, the big issue was the motherboard and ram, which started acting faulty right after this, so i had to reduce 4x4 ddr3 ram to 2x4 as 2 sticks were faulty right after this. Made a frankenstein browsing station with no case and used parts from old laptops/desktops i had around (storage, display, sound system, mouse/keyboard, etc). This experiment died 2 weeks ago and survived for roughly 2 years, the 2 last ram sticks went RIP and i have no clue why. But i suspect it might have been damage from cats or someone hit the ram sticks with an object as people in my home have the tendency to throw random stuff across rooms, since they were exposed, receiving an impact from another object could be enough to permanently damage the sticks... System powers on, but it fails to show display and the number the mobo gives is related to ram not being present. Experiment was being used by my father who is retired, he has a decent phone for everything he needs but for some he enjoyed from time to time to sit down and go watch videos on that thing. It had a purpose till the very end. The sad thing is that the CPU is still rocking, but since i don't have anymore parts to fix the problem, i'm stuck with this piece of hardware that will not get used unless i invest money into old hardware. Which is... illogical. And selling the CPU will not net me any money, last i checked it was going for less than 20 bucks in my area, and this was 2 years ago before doing the experiment.

comments.text:
Probably before your time, but the ATI 9700 Pro was absolutely more significant than the 1080 Ti.
The 9700 & 9800 series were based on the same GPU, and they constantly got different models from all sorts of brands.

It was the peak of crazy CGI GPU box art + extra letters shoved into model names because every card manufacturer was trying to jump in and get attention.  The official GPU name from ATI itself already had a ton of variants (plain, Pro, XT, XL, and SE) within a given number (9700, 9800, etc.), and the manufacturers added their own crap on top of that.

You could also fairly easily overclock or unlock many of these cards, so you could save money buy getting a cheaper card and unlock and overclock it to match or exceed the top end offerings.

We haven't seen anything like it in the industry since.

comments.text: Here's a generation-to-generation comparison:  The 1080Ti is roughly 67% faster than the previous generation consumer flagship, the 980Ti, and has almost twice the VRAM with 11GB vs 6GB.  The 980Ti launched in July 2015 for $649.  The 1080Ti launched in March 2017 for $699, just $50 more.  Adjusted for inflation, that difference is probably near zero.  That will never happen again.  The 2080Ti launched in September 2018 and is only 33% faster than the 1080Ti, has the same size VRAM buffer, and retailed for $999, $300 more than the 1080Ti.  Half the performance gain for six times the price increase.  Adding the 3080ti to this analysis would be pointless because it was not the consumer flagship.  But if we go to the 3090Ti, we see a card that gets an 80% performance uplift over the 2080Ti, and more than doubles the VRAM, but for $1999, which is 3-1/3 times the price increase of the 2080Ti over the 1080Ti and a mindblowing 20 times larger price increase compared to the 1080Ti over the 980Ti.

@hanswurst3811  Then you either had it set up wrong or tried very few games. Most games saw a sizeable increase in FPS but sometimes the same or worse 1% lows that no one paid attention to back then. You just needed to pay attention to forums to setup profiles on what methods worked best with different games. If all you did was turn it on or off you were doing it wrong.

In the early days SLI gave massive boosts because latency wasn't as critical as it is with today's bandwidth needs, and developer support was much more prevalent. I ran dual VooDoo 2s, 8800GTs, 280s, 480s, 970s, and 1080TIs. It was only with the 970s and 1080TIs that I ever had to disable a card with certain poorly optimized games.

My problem is, by calling the 1080ti a mistake justifies the higher prices of current cards.
Yeah, I bought a few 1080ti's back in the day. I still have a couple on my desk & they're great cards. However, the people and you, and other Youtubers who say the 1080ti was a mistake or ahead of its time aren't aware of the limits of die real estate or the fundamental shift in how GPU's work. Now there are games that have R/T almost baked into them and how frame generation is becoming a requirement. The price & performance of the 2080ti suffered with the R/T and Tensor cores being added to the die. The higher price of larger dies is compounded by poorer yields. This inflated the die size which made the final product more expensive.

Imagine where the 1080ti would be today if Nvidia had continued to stick to brute force through Shader core performance.

comments.text:
There was no IPC increase from maxwell to pascal. What actually happened is Nvidia skipped two process nodes, they skipped 22nm and 20nm and went straight to 16nm. 
The pricing was horrible too. The gtx 1080 is a sub-mid-range chip (312mm^2 die size out of 858mm^2 reticle limit) and costed 600-700$ when it should have been 350$. The gtx 1080Ti was a slightly above mid-range card that should have costed 500$ instead of 700-800$. 

During the same generation AMD was contractually obligated to use Global Foundry's horrible 14nm which couldn't run high clock speeds at all and consumed more power while also having lower transistor density.

The reason it will never happen again is because Nvidia will not ever skip 2 process nodes ever again.

The gtx 1000 series and people buying them like sliced bread are the reason that the current GPU market is the way it is. The gtx 600 series started it, the gtx 1000 series finished it.

comments.text:
@sirdetmist3204  Improvement in GPU's has slowed down mainly because we are reaching the physical limitations of silicon-based electronics. However, the reason that these cards "perform so poorly" in these games is not because they are weak because the 4090 is an unfathomably powerful behemoth of raw performance. The answer comes down simply to corporate greed.

If you haven't noticed, the quality of games, more specifically AAA titles, over the last several years has been tanking, just like the quality of movies. Even if less people buy them, the companies still make more money because in the end, they spent less money making a cheap, shitty game. Most of them have nothing more to bloat about than graphics, if even that. Meanwhile, they cut corners in the optimization department, meaning your GPU that should be easily getting 150+ FPS at 4k native ultra, is now getting 80 FPS at 1440p high, upscaled from 720p and with frame gen.

However, Nvidia loves this, which is why they feel like they can hike their prices up to whatever the fuck they want; people still buy the shit. They're trying to make $1600 GPU's the norm when in reality, you don't ACTUALLY need it to run the most demanding games and they know that. I guarantee that if people just stopped blindly giving greedy companies their money and forced game studios into a spot where they would HAVE to start utilizing the talents of their employees in every area, Nvidia would never be able to get away with this. Their high end would completely collapse at those prices, because any reasonable person who isn't an FPS-aholic wouldn't spend $1600 on a GPU when their $600 GPU is already giving them great performance at maxed out settings in every game. 

Sorry for the long ass rant. I just passionately hate the companies that brought PC gaming down to this level, because I've been in the scene for a while, and seeing this happen not only makes me sad, but also mad. If i could hate anything the most in this world it is corporate overreach like what we're seeing.
